analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare's pharmacy benefit managers from earning rebate-based income, limiting them to flat service fees.
analysis.headline: The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship from six senators, including the Senate Finance chairman and ranking member, but never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are companies that insurance plans hire to negotiate drug prices and manage prescription benefits. Many of them make part of their money by keeping a share of the rebates and discounts they extract from drug makers, so their earnings rise with drug prices rather than falling with them. This bill would make that illegal in Medicare's drug program: a PBM could be paid only a flat fee agreed to in its contract, and would have to hand any excess back to the government.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly 50 million people enrolled in the Part D drug benefit, who would benefit if the savings from lower drug prices were passed into lower premiums and cost-sharing instead of being retained as PBM profit. Taxpayers also gain, since Medicare pays a large share of Part D costs.

how_it_helps.text: PBMs under Medicare Part D could receive no income other than flat bona fide service fees specified in their contracts, and those fees could not be based on drug prices, discounts, or rebates.
Any PBM that received excess amounts would have to disgorge them to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Plan sponsors and PBMs would have to certify compliance annually to the Secretary of Health and Human Services.
The bill reached across the aisle: it was introduced by Sen. Menendez with original cosponsors including Republicans Blackburn, Marshall, and Crapo and Democrats Tester and Wyden.

analysis.who_pays: The PBM industry — dominated by three companies, CVS Caremark, Express Scripts (Cigna), and Optum Rx (UnitedHealth) — which would lose its rebate-based income stream in Medicare. Medicare drug plans would also take on new contracting and certification duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: The major pharmacy benefit manager companies

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only Medicare Part D, leaving PBM rebate practices in employer and commercial insurance untouched, and it lets plan sponsors keep taking rebates themselves, so rebates as such continue flowing — critics note this could shift rather than eliminate the middleman markup.

Insurers and PBMs argue that rebate dollars help keep monthly premiums down, and that a flat-fee model could raise premiums or weaken the incentive to negotiate aggressively on prices; the bill text allows plan sponsors to keep rebates that lower their net costs, implying the savings go to plans rather than automatically to enrollees.
The bill does not address spread pricing — the separate practice of PBMs charging plans more than they pay pharmacies — which is the other major complaint from independent pharmacies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound: a middleman paid a percentage of what it saves the drug makers has an incentive to keep prices high, and tying PBM pay to a flat fee removes that incentive in Medicare. But the bill is a partial fix — it leaves commercial insurance untouched, lets the plans themselves keep the rebates, and does not touch spread pricing — so its real-world benefit to beneficiaries depends on plans passing savings through. The main reason nothing happened was not a debate over its merits; it simply never received committee attention.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2023 by Sen. Menendez with five original cosponsors from both parties, including Sens. Blackburn, Tester, Marshall, Wyden, and Crapo.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
It gathered seven cosponsors in total, four Republicans and three Democrats.
No further action was recorded: the Finance Committee never held a markup or hearing on the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The three dominant pharmacy benefit managers kept their rebate-based Medicare revenue for another Congress, and Medicare beneficiaries kept paying prices shaped by that system.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — the bill was introduced by a Democrat with three Republicans and two Democrats as original cosponsors, and ended with 4 of 49 Senate Republicans and 3 of 48 Senate Democrats on board; no member is recorded as opposing it.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to earn income tied to drug prices, rebates, and discounts in Medicare, forcing them onto flat service fees. Their revenue currently grows with drug prices, which runs directly against enrollees' interest in lower prices.

industries.industry: Medicare drug plan sponsors (insurers offering Part D plans)
industries.note: They would face new contracting and annual certification duties, but the bill explicitly preserves their right to keep rebates and discounts that lower their net drug costs, so a key revenue stream survives — its benefit to enrollees depends on the plans passing savings along.
A PBM paid a share of drug spending has an incentive to preserve high prices; the flat-fee model targets that structure, which pharmacies have long argued squeezes their reimbursements.
